title: How do US Catholic subpopulations differ in fertility, retention, Mass attendance and politics, and which demographic channels are reshaping American Catholicism?
lede: research programme: comparative demography of US Catholic subpopulations from the GSS 1972-2024 with design-based intervals; the Catholic fertility premium has reversed among white Catholics born 1965-80 (-0.28 children vs Protestants), white Catholic retention fell to 55% for those born 1981-96 while Hispanic retention held near 71-76%, and Hispanics are now 37% of US Catholics; immigration, not Catholic fertility, held the Catholic share up from the 1990s to 2010-18 (+1.07 vs -0.37 points)
summary: An open research programme comparing Catholic subpopulations (Hispanic and non-Hispanic white, immigrant generations, birth cohorts, converts, weekly and occasional attenders) on fertility, retention, practice, belief and politics. Milestone 1 uses the General Social Survey 1972–2024 (NORC, release 3a), weighted, with 95% design-based intervals from the survey strata and PSUs. Among non-Hispanic whites aged 45+, Catholics born 1925–44 had 0.21 more children than Protestants, those born 1945–64 +0.04, and those born 1965–80 −0.28 [−0.48, −0.09]; weekly-attending Catholics have about 0.5–0.6 more children than other Catholics. Of non-Hispanic whites raised Catholic, 66%, 63% and 55% of the 1945–64, 1965–80 and 1981–96 cohorts are still Catholic; for Hispanics 74%, 76% and 71%. Hispanic Catholics are not more likely than white Catholics to attend weekly, and make up 37% of US Catholics in 2021–24 (31% in 2000–09). The GSS 2024 Catholic share (21.6%) sits above Pew's 2023–24 figure (19%). Milestone 5b: counterfactual reweighting credits first-generation immigrants with +1.07 points [0.52, 1.68] of the 1990–99 to 2010–18 change in the adult Catholic share and Catholic mothers’ higher fertility (about 1.1 times other mothers’) with −0.37 [−0.69, −0.02]; the result survives every sensitivity and an upper bound for fertility. GSS panels (same people re-asked): 95.4% of those raised Catholic say so again two years later (kappa 0.93, net −0.06 points), so recall error does not explain the 2021–24 rise in the raised-Catholic share; and people who later chose the web already reported 11 points less weekly attendance when interviewed in person, so the web attendance gap is mostly who chooses web. Limits: descriptive, not causal; ethnicity is measured only from 2000; the 2021–24 waves were mostly web, so changes since 2018 mix real change and mode effects; related-work notes come from abstracts. Reweighting the 2021–24 web respondents on demographics does not fix them: in the 2016–20 panel it removes about 40% of an 11-point attendance selection gap that is known to be pure selection, and among 2022–24 Catholics it leaves the 10-point web attendance gap unchanged, so post-2020 attendance is read from in-person interviews.
